## formal
Use the setting and notation of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.horizon-channels-of-the-linearised-gravitational-field-are-two-dimensional}: the Schwarzschild field in the static gauge of Fact \claimref{pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connection-curvature} on $r > 2M$, $f = 1 - 2M/r$, physical frame $\gamma_{a}$ of signature $(+,-,-,-)$ with $\hb^{-1}(e_{t}) = \sqrt f\,\gamma_{0}$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{r}) = \gamma_{1}/\sqrt f$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{\vartheta}) = r\gamma_{2}$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{\varphi}) = r\sin\vartheta\,\gamma_{3}$ (\claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), $\partial_{r_{*}} = f\partial_{r}$; a linearised field $\hb^{-1}(e_{\mu}) \mapsto \hb^{-1}(e_{\mu}) + \epsilon k_{\mu}$, $\epsilon^{2} = 0$, with $\Omega_{1}$ fixed by the torsion-free condition and first-order Ricci vectors $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{b})$; the even-parity field in the Regge-Wheeler gauge
\[
k_{t} = P\bigl(-\tfrac12\sqrt f\,H_{0}\gamma_{0} + \sqrt f\,H_{1}\gamma_{1}\bigr), \quad k_{r} = \tfrac12 f^{-1/2}H_{2}P\,\gamma_{1}, \quad k_{\vartheta} = \tfrac12 rKP\,\gamma_{2}, \quad k_{\varphi} = \tfrac12 r\sin\vartheta\,KP\,\gamma_{3},
\]
with $H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K$ smooth functions of $(t, r)$ and $P$ a smooth function of $\vartheta$; a prime on them is $\partial_{r}$, respectively $\partial_{\vartheta}$, and $\Delta P := P'' + \cot\vartheta\,P'$. For a separation constant $L > 2$ put $\lambda = (L - 2)/2 > 0$,
\[
V_{\mathrm{e}} = f\,\frac{2\lambda^{2}(\lambda+1)r^{3} + 6\lambda^{2}Mr^{2} + 18\lambda M^{2}r + 18M^{3}}{r^{3}(\lambda r + 3M)^{2}}, \qquad \mathcal{Z}[u] := \partial_{t}^{2}u - \partial_{r_{*}}^{2}u + V_{\mathrm{e}}u, \qquad \Psi := r\Bigl(K + \frac{fr}{\lambda r + 3M}\bigl(H_{2} - rK'\bigr)\Bigr),
\]
the Zerilli potential, operator and Zerilli-Moncrief function of that theorem.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Closed forms, for every angular function; proved by exact computation.)} With
\begin{align*}
C_{00} &= \tfrac{f}{2}H_{0}'' + \tfrac{2r - M}{2r^{2}}H_{0}' - \partial_{t}H_{1}' - \tfrac{2r - 3M}{r^{2}f}\partial_{t}H_{1} + \tfrac{M}{2r^{2}}H_{2}' + \tfrac{1}{2f}\partial_{t}^{2}H_{2} - \tfrac{M}{r^{2}}K' + \tfrac{1}{f}\partial_{t}^{2}K, \\
C_{01} &= \partial_{t}K' + \tfrac{r - 3M}{r^{2}f}\partial_{t}K - \tfrac{1}{r}\partial_{t}H_{2}, \qquad C_{02} = \partial_{r}(fH_{1}) - \partial_{t}(H_{2} + K), \\
C_{12} &= f(H_{0}' - K') - \partial_{t}H_{1} - \tfrac{r - 3M}{r^{2}}H_{0} + \tfrac{r - M}{r^{2}}H_{2}, \\
C_{11} &= \tfrac{f}{2}H_{0}'' + \tfrac{3M}{2r^{2}}H_{0}' - \partial_{t}H_{1}' - \tfrac{M}{r^{2}f}\partial_{t}H_{1} + \tfrac{2r - 3M}{2r^{2}}H_{2}' + \tfrac{1}{2f}\partial_{t}^{2}H_{2} - \tfrac{2r - 3M}{r^{2}}K' - fK'', \\
C_{22} &= \tfrac{f}{2r}(H_{0}' + H_{2}') - \tfrac{1}{r}\partial_{t}H_{1} + \tfrac{1}{r^{2}}(H_{2} - K) - \tfrac{2r - 3M}{r^{2}}K' - \tfrac{f}{2}K'' + \tfrac{1}{2f}\partial_{t}^{2}K,
\end{align*}
the first-order Ricci vectors are
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{0}) &= \bigl(PC_{00} + \tfrac{H_{0}}{2r^{2}}\Delta P\bigr)\gamma_{0} - \bigl(PC_{01} + \tfrac{H_{1}}{2r^{2}}\Delta P\bigr)\gamma_{1} + \tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}C_{02}\,\gamma_{2}, \\
\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{1}) &= \bigl(PC_{01} + \tfrac{H_{1}}{2r^{2}}\Delta P\bigr)\gamma_{0} + \bigl(PC_{11} - \tfrac{H_{2}}{2r^{2}}\Delta P\bigr)\gamma_{1} + \tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}C_{12}\,\gamma_{2}, \\
\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{2}) &= -\tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}C_{02}\,\gamma_{0} + \tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}C_{12}\,\gamma_{1} + \bigl(PC_{22} - \tfrac{K}{2r^{2}}\Delta P + \tfrac{H_{0} - H_{2}}{2r^{2}}P''\bigr)\gamma_{2}, \\
\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{3}) &= \bigl(PC_{22} - \tfrac{K}{2r^{2}}\Delta P + \tfrac{H_{0} - H_{2}}{2r^{2}}\cot\vartheta\,P'\bigr)\gamma_{3},
\end{align*}
at every radius of the exterior and every polar angle with $\sin\vartheta \neq 0$. The evidence: $\mathcal{R}_{1}$ at a point is a linear function of the second-order jet of $k$ there, so both sides are bilinear in the second-order jets of $(H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K)$ and of $P$ at the point; on the $24$ basis jets of the first and the $3$ basis jets $(P, P', P'')$ of the second every one of the sixteen components agrees as an identity in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[z, z^{-1}, (1 - z^{2})^{-1}, s, s^{-1}, c]/(c^{2} + s^{2} - 1)$, $z = \sqrt f$ with $r = 2M/(1 - z^{2})$, $s = \sin\vartheta$, $c = \cos\vartheta$, at $M = 1$; the expressions are homogeneous under $(t, r, M) \mapsto (at, ar, aM)$. No separation constant enters and no degree bound is used.
\item \emph{(Odd parity, without the degree bound; proved by exact computation.)} The closed forms of clause (1) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.horizon-channels-of-the-linearised-gravitational-field-are-two-dimensional} hold as identities in the same ring, on the $12$ basis jets of $(h_{0}, h_{1})$, the $2$ basis data of $(S, S')$ and two values of $L$ (both sides are of degree one in $L$, which enters through $S''$ alone); so that clause holds at every radius and polar angle without the degree bound in $\cot\vartheta$ argued there.
\item \emph{(The radial system; proved from (1).)} Let $P$ be a nonzero solution of $P'' + \cot\vartheta\,P' + LP = 0$ with $L \notin \{0, 2\}$. Then $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{b}) = 0$ for all $b$ if and only if
\[
E_{1} := C_{00} - \tfrac{L}{2r^{2}}H_{0}, \quad E_{2} := C_{01} - \tfrac{L}{2r^{2}}H_{1}, \quad E_{3} := C_{02}, \quad E_{4} := C_{12}, \quad E_{5} := C_{11} + \tfrac{L}{2r^{2}}H_{2}, \quad E_{6} := H_{0} - H_{2}, \quad E_{7} := C_{22} + \tfrac{L}{2r^{2}}K
\]
all vanish.
\item \emph{(The converse: every solution of the Zerilli equation is a master function; proved, identically.)} For a smooth function $\Phi(t, r)$ let
\begin{align*}
K &= \frac{\lambda(\lambda+1)r^{2} + 3\lambda Mr + 6M^{2}}{r^{2}(\lambda r + 3M)}\Phi + f\Phi', \qquad H_{1} = \partial_{t}\bigl(r\Phi' + a\Phi\bigr), \quad a := \frac{\lambda r^{2} - 3\lambda Mr - 3M^{2}}{(r - 2M)(\lambda r + 3M)}, \\
H_{0} = H_{2} &= -\frac{\lambda^{2}(\lambda+1)r^{3} + 3\lambda^{2}Mr^{2} + 9\lambda M^{2}r + 9M^{3}}{r^{2}(\lambda r + 3M)^{2}}\Phi + \frac{\lambda r^{2} - \lambda Mr + 3M^{2}}{r(\lambda r + 3M)}\Phi' + (r - 2M)\Phi''.
\end{align*}
Then, identically in $\Phi$: $\Psi = (\lambda + 1)\Phi$; $E_{2} = E_{3} = E_{6} = 0$; $E_{4} = -(r\partial_{r} + a)\mathcal{Z}[\Phi]$; $E_{7} = -\tfrac12\partial_{r}\mathcal{Z}[\Phi] + b\,\mathcal{Z}[\Phi]$ with $b = \bigl(\lambda(\lambda - 1)r^{2} + 9\lambda Mr + 12M^{2}\bigr)/\bigl(2r(r - 2M)(\lambda r + 3M)\bigr)$; and $E_{1}$, $E_{5}$ are second-order differential operators in $r$ applied to $\mathcal{Z}[\Phi]$, with leading coefficient $-r/2$ and coefficients regular on $r > 2M$. Hence if $\mathcal{Z}[\Phi] = 0$ the field is an even-parity vacuum solution with Zerilli-Moncrief function $(\lambda + 1)\Phi$: every solution $\Psi$ of the Zerilli equation is the Zerilli-Moncrief function of the vacuum solution built from $\Phi = \Psi/(\lambda + 1)$. No condition on the time dependence is used.
\item \emph{(An oscillating channel: the master function carries the whole field; proved, identically.)} On functions with $\partial_{t}^{2} = -\omega^{2}$, $\omega$ real and nonzero, let $(H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K)$ solve $E_{1} = \cdots = E_{7} = 0$ and write $H = H_{0} = H_{2}$. Then $E_{3}$, $E_{4}$ and $\partial_{t}E_{2}$ are the first-order system
\[
K' = -\frac{r - 3M}{r^{2}f}K + \frac{H}{r} - \frac{\lambda + 1}{r^{2}\omega^{2}}\partial_{t}H_{1}, \qquad H' = K' + \frac{1}{f}\Bigl(\partial_{t}H_{1} - \frac{2M}{r^{2}}H\Bigr), \qquad H_{1}' = \frac{1}{f}\Bigl(\partial_{t}H + \partial_{t}K - \frac{2M}{r^{2}}H_{1}\Bigr);
\]
under it $E_{7}$ becomes $(2r^{3})^{-1}$ times the algebraic relation
\[
\mathrm{Rel} := -(\lambda r + 3M)H + \frac{\lambda r(r - 2M) + M(r - 3M) - \omega^{2}r^{4}}{r - 2M}K + \frac{M(\lambda + 1) - \omega^{2}r^{3}}{r\omega^{2}}\partial_{t}H_{1} = 0,
\]
$E_{1}$, $E_{5}$ and $\partial_{r}\mathrm{Rel}$ become multiples of $\mathrm{Rel}$ with coefficients regular on $r > 2M$, and so does $\mathcal{Z}[\Psi]$: the vacuum equations imply the Zerilli equation for $\Psi$. Under the first-order system alone, $(\lambda + 1)(K, H, H_{1})$ is the field built in (4) from $\Phi = \Psi$. So a vacuum solution of the channel with $\Psi = 0$ vanishes, and $(H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K) \mapsto \Psi$ is a bijection from the even-parity vacuum solutions of the channel in the Regge-Wheeler gauge onto the solutions of the Zerilli equation in the channel, with inverse $\Psi \mapsto$ the field of (4) for $\Phi = \Psi/(\lambda + 1)$.
\item \emph{(At the horizon.)} By (4), (5) and clauses (4) and (5) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.horizon-channels-of-the-linearised-gravitational-field-are-two-dimensional} ($V_{\mathrm{e}}/f$ regular and positive at $r = 2M$, $V_{\mathrm{e}} = O(e^{2\kappa r_{*}})$), every even-parity channel with $\ell \geq 2$ and real $\omega \neq 0$ in the Regge-Wheeler gauge is carried by one function obeying a two-dimensional equation in $(t, r_{*})$ whose potential vanishes at the horizon at the rate $e^{2\kappa r_{*}}$, as the odd-parity channels are: the cited fact (C3) of that theorem is proved, and its clause (3), computed at sample points, is superseded by (5). The scope stated there is unchanged: the static frame; $\ell \geq 2$; oscillating channels; (C1) (completeness of the tensor harmonics) and (C2) (reachability of the Regge-Wheeler gauge) remain cited from memory and enter the phrase ``every channel''; the current-boson identification and the partial-wave lift of joint J3 (\claimref{hawking.joint-j3-s-wave-reduction}) are not derived.
\end{enumerate}
The identities of (4) and (5) are computed at $M = 1$ in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[r, \lambda, w][r^{-1}, (r - 2)^{-1}, (\lambda r + 3)^{-1}, w^{-1}]$, $w = \omega^{2}$, in which only these units are inverted; every expression is homogeneous under $(t, r, M) \mapsto (at, ar, aM)$ with $H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K$ of weight $0$ and $\Phi$, $\Psi$ of weight $1$, which gives general $M$. On $r > 2M$ with $\lambda > 0$ none of the inverted quantities vanishes.

## technical
The stored result on the linearised gravitational field around a static black hole proved that each odd-parity channel is one function obeying a two-dimensional wave equation, and for even parity showed only, at two sample points, that the vacuum equations imply the Zerilli equation; that the Zerilli function carries the whole channel was cited. This result closes the even-parity case. First, the first-order Ricci vectors of the even-parity field are computed in closed form, as identities in the radius and the polar angle together and for an arbitrary angular function, by running the stored linearisation with coefficients in an exact ring in which only $\sqrt f$, $1 - f$ and $\sin\vartheta$ are ever inverted. The same computation turns the stored odd-parity closed forms into identities in both variables, so the degree bound that was argued there is not needed. Second, for a harmonic with $\ell \geq 2$ the vacuum equations are seven radial equations. Third, from any function $\Phi$ a field is written down whose seven equations are explicit differential operators applied to the Zerilli operator on $\Phi$, and whose Zerilli-Moncrief function is $(\lambda + 1)\Phi$: a solution of the Zerilli equation gives a vacuum solution, with no condition on its time dependence. Fourth, on a channel of nonzero real frequency the vacuum equations amount to a first-order system in the radius and one algebraic relation, the system preserves the relation, the Zerilli equation follows from them identically, and the field equals the field rebuilt from its own master function. So the master function is a bijection between even-parity vacuum solutions of the channel and solutions of the Zerilli equation, and with the stored horizon values of the potential each even-parity channel is a two-dimensional mode at the horizon in the static frame. What remains outside is what was outside for odd parity: the completeness of the tensor harmonics and the reachability of the gauge, both cited; the cases $\ell = 0, 1$; charts regular across the horizon; and the identification of a channel with a current boson, which stays a premise.

## lay
A small ripple in the gravitational field around a black hole can be sorted into simple patterns, two for each pitch and each angular shape. For one of the two kinds it was already shown that a single wave on a line, running towards or away from the horizon, carries the whole pattern. For the other kind that was known in one direction only, and at a few test points. This result finishes it: every such wave on a line gives a ripple that solves the field equations, every ripple of that kind is rebuilt exactly from its wave, and close to the horizon the wave moves freely. The calculation is exact at every distance and every angle, not sampled. Two textbook facts about sorting ripples into patterns are still taken on trust.

## one-liner
For the even-parity linearised gravitational field on the static Schwarzschild exterior in the Regge-Wheeler gauge, $\ell \geq 2$: closed forms of the first-order Ricci vectors as identities in radius and angle; every solution $\Psi$ of the Zerilli equation is the Zerilli-Moncrief function of the vacuum field rebuilt from $\Psi/(\lambda+1)$, each vacuum equation being a differential multiple of the Zerilli operator; and on a channel of real frequency $\omega \neq 0$ the vacuum equations imply the Zerilli equation and the field is the rebuilt one, so the master function carries the whole channel (the stored cited fact (C3) proved; (C1), (C2) remain cited).

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{Setting.} The linearisation is that of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.horizon-channels-of-the-linearised-gravitational-field-are-two-dimensional}: the static coframe of Fact \claimref{pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connection-curvature}, $g_{\mu} \mapsto g_{\mu} + \epsilon k_{\mu}$, $\Omega(e_{\mu}) \mapsto \Omega(e_{\mu}) + \epsilon\Omega_{1}(e_{\mu})$, $\epsilon^{2} = 0$; $\Omega_{1}$ is the unique solution of the first-order torsion-free condition $\Omega_{1}(e_{\mu}) \cdot g_{\nu} - \Omega_{1}(e_{\nu}) \cdot g_{\mu} = -(D_{\mu}k_{\nu} - D_{\nu}k_{\mu})$ (\claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), and $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{b})$ is the first-order part of the Ricci vector of the curvature operator in the store's sign. The stated $k_{\mu}$ give the first-order metric $-fH_{0}P\,dt^{2} - 2H_{1}P\,dt\,dr - f^{-1}H_{2}P\,dr^{2} - r^{2}KP\,(d\vartheta^{2} + \sin^{2}\vartheta\,d\varphi^{2})$.

\emph{Why a basis of jets decides (1) and (2).} $\Omega_{1}$ at a point is a linear function of $k$ and its first derivatives there (the torsion system is algebraic in $\Omega_{1}$, with the invertible matrix of the background torsion map), and $\mathcal{R}_{1}$ is a linear function of $\Omega_{1}$, its first derivatives and $k$; so $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\gamma_{b})$ at a point is a linear function of the second-order jet of $k$ at that point. For the even-parity field each component of $k_{\mu}$ is a background function times a product $H(t,r)P(\vartheta)$, whose second-order jet at the point is a bilinear function of the second-order jets of $H$ and of $P$ there. The displayed right-hand sides are bilinear in the same jets. So the two sides agree for all smooth $H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K, P$ at the point as soon as they agree on a basis: the six monomials $t^{p}(r - r_{0})^{q}$, $p + q \leq 2$, for each of the four functions, and the three monomials $1$, $\vartheta - \vartheta_{0}$, $\tfrac12(\vartheta - \vartheta_{0})^{2}$ for $P$. Nothing is assumed of $P$: the term $P''$ is independent data, so no separation constant and no degree count in $L$ or in $\cot\vartheta$ enters.

\emph{Why the comparison is an identity in the radius and the angle.} The check runs the linearisation with jets whose coefficients lie in $U = \mathbb{Q}[z, z^{-1}, (1 - z^{2})^{-1}, s, s^{-1}, c]/(c^{2} + s^{2} - 1)$, the base point being $r_{0} = 2/(1 - z^{2})$, $\sqrt{f(r_{0})} = z$, $\sin\vartheta_{0} = s$, $\cos\vartheta_{0} = c$ ($M = 1$). An element of $U$ is stored as a polynomial numerator, reduced by $c^{2} = 1 - s^{2}$ to degree at most one in $c$, over a monomial $z^{a}(1 - z^{2})^{b}s^{e}$; such a representation is zero only if the numerator is, since $z$, $1 - z^{2}$ and $s$ are not zero divisors. The implementation inverts only rational multiples of monomials in $z$, $1 - z^{2}$ and $s$ and raises an error otherwise; the computation completes, so every division made was by such a unit (the pivots of the torsion system are monomials in the frame components $z$, $1/z$, $r_{0}$, $r_{0}s$, as its homogeneity under independent rescalings of the four frame vectors requires). $U$ maps to the functions on $\{2M < r,\ \sin\vartheta \neq 0\}$ by evaluation, and the units are nonzero there, so an equality in $U$ is an equality of functions at every radius of the exterior and every such angle. All sixteen components are compared in each of the $72$ cases, the vanishing ones included ($72$ are nonzero). General $M$: every term of the closed forms is homogeneous under $(t, r, M) \mapsto (at, ar, aM)$ with $H_{0}, H_{1}, H_{2}, K$ of weight $0$ (weight $-2$ for $C_{00}, C_{01}, C_{11}, C_{22}$ and the $\Delta P$ terms, $-1$ for $C_{02}, C_{12}$, whose prefactor $1/(2r\sqrt f)$ has weight $-1$), and so is $\mathcal{R}_{1}$, the constant dilation of the chart being a displacement (clause (e) of the Definition) that carries the field of mass $M$ to a constant multiple of the field of mass $aM$; a sampled control at masses $\tfrac98$ and $\tfrac{25}{18}$ with generic jets is in the check. This proves (1).

\emph{(2).} The same computation with the odd-parity field of the cited theorem, $k_{\varphi} = S(f^{-1/2}h_{0}\gamma_{0} - f^{1/2}h_{1}\gamma_{1})$: its closed forms contain $L$ through $E_{t}$ and $E_{r}$, and they were derived for $S'' = \cot\vartheta\,S' - LS$. Both sides are linear in the second-order jet of $S$, hence, with $S''$ so expressed, of degree one in $L$ for fixed $(S, S')$; they agree in $U$ for $L = \tfrac72$ and $L = 6$ on the $12$ basis jets of $(h_{0}, h_{1})$ and the two basis data of $(S, S')$ ($48$ cases, $56$ nonzero components counting the symmetric partners), hence for every $L$, radius and angle.

\emph{(3).} With $\Delta P = -LP$ the components of (1) are $P E_{1}$, $\mp P E_{2}$, $\pm\tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}E_{3}$, $\tfrac{P'}{2r\sqrt f}E_{4}$, $P E_{5}$, and $P E_{7} + \tfrac{1}{2r^{2}}E_{6}P''$, $P E_{7} + \tfrac{1}{2r^{2}}E_{6}\cot\vartheta\,P'$, where $E_{j}$ depend on $(t, r)$ only. If all $E_{j}$ vanish, so does $\mathcal{R}_{1}$. Conversely let $\mathcal{R}_{1} = 0$. $P$ is not identically zero, and neither is $P'$ since $L \neq 0$; so $E_{1} = E_{2} = E_{3} = E_{4} = E_{5} = 0$. The difference of the last two components is $\tfrac{1}{2r^{2}}E_{6}(P'' - \cot\vartheta\,P')$. If $P'' = \cot\vartheta\,P'$ identically, the equation of $P$ gives $2\cot\vartheta\,P' = -LP$, so $P = C\cos^{n}\vartheta$ with $n = L/2$ on an interval where $\cos\vartheta \neq 0$, and then $P'' + \cot\vartheta\,P' + LP = n(n-1)C\cos^{n-2}\vartheta\,\sin^{2}\vartheta$, which vanishes identically only for $n \in \{0, 1\}$, that is $L \in \{0, 2\}$. So for $L \notin \{0, 2\}$, $E_{6} = 0$ and then $E_{7} = 0$.

\emph{The differential algebra used for (4) and (5).} Let $A = \mathbb{Q}[r, \lambda, w][r^{-1}, (r - 2)^{-1}, (\lambda r + 3)^{-1}, w^{-1}]$, with $d/dr$ acting in the evident way, and consider linear forms with coefficients in $A$ in symbols $\partial_{t}^{p}\partial_{r}^{q}X$ for named functions $X$; $\partial_{r}$ and $\partial_{t}$ act on them by the Leibniz rule. A linear form is a linear differential expression in the functions $X$, and it is the zero form only if all its coefficients are zero in $A$ (numerators compared after bringing to a common denominator). The check evaluates the closed forms of (1) on such linear forms with $M = 1$, $f = (r - 2)/r$; every identity below is an equality of linear forms, hence an identity for arbitrary smooth functions at every $r > 2$, $\lambda > 0$, $w > 0$, where the inverted quantities do not vanish. Homogeneity as in (1), with $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ of weight $1$, gives general $M$.

\emph{(4).} Put $Z := \mathcal{Z}[\Phi]$, so that $\partial_{t}^{2}\Phi = f(f\Phi')' - V_{\mathrm{e}}\Phi + Z$, and substitute this (and its $t$- and $r$-derivatives) for every symbol $\partial_{t}^{p}\partial_{r}^{q}\Phi$ with $p \geq 2$ in the linear forms $E_{j}$ of the stated field. The substitution is an identity for every smooth $\Phi$, with $Z$ standing for $\mathcal{Z}[\Phi]$. The result, computed by the check: no symbol of $\Phi$ remains in any $E_{j}$; $E_{2}$, $E_{3}$, $E_{6}$ are zero (for $E_{3}$: $fH_{1} = \partial_{t}(fr\Phi' + fa\Phi)$ and $H_{2} + K$ are arranged so that $\partial_{r}(fH_{1}) = \partial_{t}(H_{2} + K)$; they contain no second time derivative, so the substitution is not used); $E_{4} = -(rZ' + aZ)$ and $E_{7} = -\tfrac12 Z' + bZ$ with the stated $a$, $b$; $E_{1}$ and $E_{5}$ are combinations of $Z$, $Z'$, $Z''$ with coefficients in $A$ and coefficient $-r/2$ of $Z''$. The Zerilli-Moncrief function of the field is computed directly, without substitution: $r\bigl(K + \tfrac{fr}{\lambda r + 3}(H_{2} - rK')\bigr) = (\lambda + 1)\Phi$ as linear forms (the terms in $\Phi'$ and $\Phi''$ cancel). With a potential differing by $f/r^{2}$ a term in $\Phi$ is left in $E_{4}$, so the test is sensitive to the potential. If $\mathcal{Z}[\Phi] = 0$ all $E_{j}$ vanish and by (3) the field is a vacuum solution; $\mathcal{Z}$ is linear, so $\Phi = \Psi/(\lambda + 1)$ solves the Zerilli equation when $\Psi$ does, and $\lambda + 1 = L/2 \neq 0$.

\emph{(5).} Let the field solve $E_{1} = \cdots = E_{7} = 0$ on the channel and write $H$ for $H_{0} = H_{2}$ ($E_{6}$). As linear forms, $E_{3} = f\,(H_{1}' - \rho_{1})$ and $E_{4} = f\,\bigl((H' - K') - (\rho_{H} - \rho_{K})\bigr)$, and, using $\partial_{t}^{2} = -\omega^{2}$, $\partial_{t}E_{2} = -\omega^{2}(K' - \rho_{K})$, where $\rho_{K}, \rho_{H}, \rho_{1}$ are the right-hand sides of the displayed first-order system (checked as equalities of linear forms). Since $f \neq 0$ and $\omega \neq 0$, the solution satisfies the system. Call \emph{reduction} the replacement of every symbol $\partial_{t}^{p}\partial_{r}^{q}X$, $X \in \{K, H, H_{1}\}$, with $q \geq 1$ by the corresponding derivative of the right-hand side, and of $\partial_{t}^{2}$ by $-\omega^{2}$, until only $K, H, H_{1}, \partial_{t}K, \partial_{t}H, \partial_{t}H_{1}$ remain; on the solution every expression equals its reduction. The check computes: $E_{2}, E_{3}, E_{4}, E_{6}$ reduce to zero; $E_{7}$ reduces to $\mathrm{Rel}/(2r^{3})$, a combination of $H$, $K$ and $\partial_{t}H_{1}$ with the stated coefficients, in which the coefficient of $H$, $-(\lambda r + 3)/(2r^{3})$, is a unit of $A$; $E_{1}$, $E_{5}$, $\partial_{r}\mathrm{Rel}$ and $\mathcal{Z}[\Psi]$ each reduce to $\mu\,\mathrm{Rel}$ with $\mu \in A$ (the quotient of the coefficients of $H$), a function regular on $r > 2$. So on the solution $\mathrm{Rel} = 0$ and $\mathcal{Z}[\Psi] = 0$: the Zerilli equation follows from the vacuum equations, identically. Finally $(\lambda + 1)K - K[\Psi]$, $(\lambda + 1)H - H[\Psi]$ and $(\lambda + 1)H_{1} - H_{1}[\Psi]$, where $K[\cdot], H[\cdot], H_{1}[\cdot]$ are the operators of (4), reduce to zero, without use of $\mathrm{Rel}$; so on the solution $(\lambda + 1)(K, H, H_{1})$ is the field of (4) built from $\Psi$, and $\Psi = 0$ forces the field to vanish. With (4): the map to $\Psi$ lands in the solutions of the Zerilli equation of the channel, is injective, and is onto with the stated inverse, because the field of (4) built from a channel solution $\Phi$ lies in the channel (its operators commute with $\partial_{t}$), solves the vacuum equations and has master function $(\lambda + 1)\Phi$. (That $E_{1}$, $E_{5}$ and $\partial_{r}\mathrm{Rel}$ are multiples of $\mathrm{Rel}$ is not needed for the bijection; it records that the first-order system with the one relation is the whole content of the seven equations on the channel: by the equalities above, the system gives $E_{3} = E_{4} = \partial_{t}E_{2} = 0$, hence $E_{2} = 0$ since $\omega \neq 0$, and with $\mathrm{Rel} = 0$ it gives $E_{1} = E_{5} = E_{7} = 0$.)

\emph{(6).} By (3) and (5), in the Regge-Wheeler gauge an even-parity vacuum solution on an oscillating channel with $L = \ell(\ell+1)$, $\ell \geq 2$, is the field of (4) built from a solution of $\mathcal{Z}[\Psi] = 0$, and conversely. Clause (5) of the cited theorem gives $V_{\mathrm{e}}/f$ regular and positive at $r = 2M$ and $V_{\mathrm{e}} = O(e^{2\kappa r_{*}})$ as $r_{*} \to -\infty$, so $\Psi$ obeys the free two-dimensional equation there, as stated in that clause conditionally on (C3); (C3) is the surjectivity proved in (4) together with the injectivity of (5). The reductions (C1) and (C2), from a general linearised field to the axisymmetric representative of one harmonic in the Regge-Wheeler gauge, are not touched by this proof and remain cited from memory.
